newsitem.title: ITALY: Presiding judge calls Priebke verdict "painful".
newsitem.headline: Presiding judge calls Priebke verdict "painful".

text.p: The presiding judge who ruled that former Nazi SS captain Erich Priebke was guilty but could not be jailed for his part in Italy's worst wartime atrocity stood by his decision on Monday but said it had been "painful".

Military court president Agostino Quistelli said in a 123-page document explaining the verdict that Priebke, 83, would have been liable to nearly 30 years in jail if a statute of limitations had not expired.
He told reporters it had been "a painful verdict" which had split the three-judge bench two-to-one.
The ruling, handed down on August 1, unleashed a torrent of anger among relatives of the 335 men and boys rounded up and shot by the Nazis in the Ardeatine Caves near Rome in 1944.
Protesters besieged the courtroom for several hours, trapping Priebke inside until he was finally re-arrested by Italian authorities and transferred to a civilian jail.

Quistelli, himself under siege and widely criticised for the verdict, was given police protection. Lawyers for relatives of the victims have appealed, questioning the competence of the judges, and the prosecution has also challenged the ruling.
The re-arrest was made pending a German request to extradite Priebke for trial there. No decision has yet been reached and he is still held in the Regina Coeli (Queen of Heavens) prison.

Italy's highest appeals court, the court of cassation, called earlier this month for a constitutional ruling on whether Priebke was legitimately re-arrested. His lawyer said that meant he would have to stay in prison until a verdict was reached.

Quistelli's report, full of complicated legal language, hedged the question of whether Priebke had demonstrated cruelty, saying it could not be certain that the victims were made to clamber on top of piles of bodies to be shot themselves.

He called the atrocity a war crime and said Priebke would have faced a jail sentence of at least 21 years and "much closer to 30 years", with the attenuating circumstances equivalent to a life sentence, "if he had been brought to trial within a few years of the event and not half a century afterwards".

Priebke said he shot two people and Quistelli's report said he had also admitted taking part in drawing up the lists of victims the night before. The massacre was a reprisal for a partisan attack the previous day which killed 33 Nazi soldiers.

But he said Priebke, who lived quietly under his own name in Argentina for nearly half a century, now had a "virtually non-existent capacity to commit a crime". His good behaviour since the war was also taken into account in the verdict.

The Court of Cassation is due to discuss the appeals in October. Italy has said Priebke cannot be extradited while appeals remain open and that it would need permission from Argentina, which has barred his return, to hand him over to a third country.
